07.01.title: Particle kinematics
07.01.html:
Dynamics starts with describing motion before asking what causes it. A car on a roundabout, a cyclist braking into a bend and a phone logging GPS points are all “particles”: objects whose size doesn’t matter for the question. Kinematics gives their velocity and acceleration, and the right choice of coordinates makes the physics obvious.

Cartesian coordinates

Position r(t)=(x,y). Velocity and acceleration are time derivatives:

v=r˙,a=v˙=r¨.

Simple, but it hides what a driver feels: braking versus turning.

Path coordinates

Use a unit tangent et​ along the path and a unit normal en​ towards the centre of curvature. With speed v and local radius of curvature ρ:

v=vet​,a=v˙et​+ρv2​en​.

The tangential part at​=v˙ changes the speed. The normal part an​=v2/ρ changes the direction. On a straight, ρ→∞ and an​=0. At steady speed round a circle, at​=0 but an​=v2/R still points inward.

Polar coordinates

For things that swing or spin (a radar tracking a plane, a bead sliding on a rotating rod), use r and θ:

ar​=r¨−rθ˙2,aθ​=rθ¨+2r˙θ˙.

The −rθ˙2 term is the centripetal part; 2r˙θ˙ is the Coriolis part (more in 07.12).

From measured data

A GPS log gives positions at discrete times. Differentiating once gives velocity, twice gives acceleration. Central differences work, but every differentiation amplifies measurement noise. Smoothing first trades noise for a little lag.

Worked exampleA roundabout and a GPS track

  1. A car circles a 50 m roundabout at 10 m/s, logged at 10 Hz. Central differences give at​=5×10−14, an​=1.9997 m/s² against v2/R=2, and a radius of 50.000 m.
  2. A cyclist brakes at 0.3 m/s² from 12 m/s through a 30 m bend, logged once a second. Mid-bend at 12 s: speed 8.29 m/s (true 8.40), at​=−0.27 (true −0.30), an​=2.29 m/s² (true 2.35). One-second sampling cuts corners.
  3. Add 0.5 m of GPS noise and the tangential acceleration even comes out with the wrong sign (+0.56). Accelerations from raw GPS need filtering.
  4. Polar check: r=2+0.5t, θ=0.8t at t=1.3 s gives ar​=−1.696 and aθ​=0.800 m/s², by formula and by numerical differentiation.

Exercise 1A motorway exit

A car leaves a motorway at 100 km/h on an exit ramp with a 120 m radius and brakes at 2 m/s². What is its total acceleration as it enters the curve? How fast could it go round the curve if the tyres can deliver 0.6 g in total and it stops braking?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. v=27.78 m/s, so an​=27.782/120=6.43 m/s².
  2. Total: 6.432+22​=6.73 m/s², about 0.69 g. Too much for 0.6 g of grip: the driver should have braked before the curve.
  3. Without braking: v2/120=0.6⋅9.81 gives v=26.6 m/s =95.7 km/h.

quiz.explain: v2/ρ.

quiz.explain: Combine at​ and an​.

quiz.explain: v=aρ​.

quiz.explain: Only the normal part remains.

07.02.title: Newton's second law
07.02.html:
Kinematics describes motion; Newton’s second law explains it. The method is the same one used in statics (Phase 05): cut the body free, draw every force acting on it, and add them up. The only difference is that the sum is no longer zero. It equals mass times acceleration.

The law

For a particle of constant mass m:

∑F=ma.

It holds in an inertial frame, one that isn’t accelerating or rotating (the ground is close enough for most engineering). Written in components it gives one equation per direction, the same as equilibrium equations but with max​, may​ on the right.

The recipe

  1. Choose the body and draw its free-body diagram: gravity, contact forces, friction, drag, thrust.
  2. Choose coordinates (Cartesian, path or polar: whichever makes the acceleration simple).
  3. Write ∑F=ma in each direction.
  4. Solve: either algebraically, or, if forces depend on velocity or position, as a differential equation integrated in time.

Drag

Air drag on a fast body grows with the square of speed and points against the velocity:

FD​=−21​ρCD​A∣v∣v.

Now the equations couple x and y and have no simple closed-form solution. Integrate them numerically, with the RK4 method from Phase 04.

A ski jumper

Cut the jumper free in flight: gravity mg down and drag against the velocity (real jumpers also generate lift, which we leave out). Without drag, the path is the parabola of Phase 02. With drag, the jumper lands sooner and slower. The parabola is a test case: the simulation with CD​A=0 must reproduce it exactly.

Worked exampleDrag and the ski jumper

m=65 kg, v0​=25 m/s, take-off 11° down, air density 1.2 kg/m³, landing slope 35°.

  1. With zero drag, RK4 with a 1 ms step matches the parabola y=vy0​t−gt2/2 to 2.5×10−12 m.
  2. Hand check for no drag: the jumper hits the slope when vy0​t−gt2/2=−tan35°⋅vx0​t, giving t=2.531 s and 75.82 m along the slope, exactly what the simulation finds.
  3. With drag: CD​A=0.3 m² lands at 67.49 m (118 km/h), 0.5 m² at 63.07 m (108 km/h), 0.8 m² at 57.62 m (97 km/h).
  4. A tighter tuck pays off. Jumpers flying well beyond 100 m on big hills do it with lift from their V-style skis.

Exercise 1A lift in a tall building

A person of 75 kg stands on a scale in a lift. What does the scale read (in newtons and in “kg”) when the lift (a) accelerates upward at 1.5 m/s², (b) moves at constant speed, (c) slows down while going up at 2 m/s²?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Free body: weight mg down, scale force N up. N−mg=ma, so N=m(g+a) with a up positive.
  2. (a) 75⋅(9.81+1.5)=848 N, reads 86.5 kg.
  3. (b) a=0: N=736 N, reads 75 kg.
  4. (c) a=−2: N=75⋅7.81=586 N, reads 59.7 kg.

quiz.explain: N=m(g+a).

quiz.q: No-drag flight time (s) of the ski jumper before landing. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: Intersect the parabola with the slope.

quiz.q: Drag force (N) on a jumper with CD​A=0.5 m² at 25 m/s in air of 1.2 kg/m³.
quiz.explain: 21​ρCD​Av2.

quiz.q: Newton’s second law in the form ∑F=ma holds in…
quiz.explain: Non-inertial frames need extra terms (07.12).

07.03.title: Work and energy
07.03.html:
Newton’s law gives the acceleration at every instant. Often you only want to know how fast something is going at a certain place: a roller coaster at the bottom of a drop, a car after braking over 30 m, a hammer as it hits a nail. Integrating F=ma along the path once and for all gives a shortcut that skips time entirely: work and energy.

The work–energy theorem

Dot mv˙=F with vdt=dr and integrate along the path from 1 to 2:

21​mv22​−21​mv12​=∫12​F⋅dr=W12​.

The change in kinetic energy equals the work done by all forces. Forces perpendicular to the motion (the normal force from a track, the tension in a pendulum string) do no work.

Conservative forces and potential energy

Some forces do work that depends only on the start and end points, not the path: gravity, springs. Their work can be stored as potential energy, Vg​=mgh and Vs​=21​kx2. If only conservative forces do work:

T+V=constant.

Friction and drag are not conservative. They take energy out, usually as heat: T2​+V2​=T1​+V1​−Wloss​.

Roller coasters

A frictionless car released at height h0​ with speed v0​ has, at height h,

v=v02​+2g(h0​−h)​.

Mass cancels and the shape of the track between doesn’t matter. The car can never climb above h0​+v02​/2g. A test: simulate the motion along the track with s¨=−gsinθ and the speeds must agree with energy everywhere.

Worked exampleThe coaster, two ways

Track profile: from 40 m down towards 10 m, a 12 m bump near x=80 m, a 17 m hill near x=150 m; 1 m/s at the top.

  1. RK4 on the path equation with a 1 ms step, 14,458 steps: largest difference from the energy speed 1.5×10−9 m/s.
  2. Speeds: 16.79 m/s at x=30 m (25 m high), 23.82 m/s = 85.8 km/h at the dip (h=10.44 m), 15.57 m/s over the last crest (h=27 m).
  3. Add rolling friction μ=0.015 and the car reaches the last crest at 14.09 m/s instead: the friction work has eaten into its energy.

Exercise 1A car brakes to a stop

A 1400 kg car brakes from 90 km/h on a level road with a constant friction force of 0.8 times its weight. How far does it travel? Then on a 10 % downhill grade?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Level: 21​mv2=μmgd, so d=v2/(2μg)=252/(2⋅0.8⋅9.81)=39.8 m. Mass cancels.
  2. Downhill, slope angle θ=arctan0.1=5.71°: gravity does positive work mgsinθd, friction μmgcosθd.
  3. d=v2/(2g(μcosθ−sinθ))=625/(2⋅9.81⋅(0.796−0.0995))=45.7 m.

quiz.explain: 2gh​.

quiz.q: Braking distance (m) from 90 km/h with friction 0.8 g on level ground. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: v2/(2μg).

quiz.q: Braking distance (m) on a 10 % downhill grade. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: Gravity helps the car along.

quiz.q: The normal force from a roller-coaster track does…
quiz.explain: F⋅dr=0.
options: Positive work on the way down
Negative work on the way up
No work, being perpendicular to the motion
Work equal to mgh

quiz.explain: Friction’s work depends on the path.

07.04.title: Impulse and momentum
07.04.html:
A collision lasts milliseconds and the forces during it are huge and hard to measure. Yet what happens afterwards is easy to predict, because Newton’s law integrated over time says the total momentum can’t change. Car crash reconstruction, billiards, railway couplings and a hammer driving a nail all use this.

Impulse

Integrate F=mv˙ over a time interval:

∫t1​t2​​Fdt=mv2​−mv1​.

The left side is the impulse: force times time. A small force for a long time does the same as a big force for a short time. That is why airbags and crumple zones save lives: they stretch the stopping time, so the force on the body drops.

Conservation of momentum

When two bodies collide, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite (Newton’s third law), so their impulses cancel. Without outside forces:

m1​v1​+m2​v2​=m1​v1′​+m2​v2′​.

Restitution

Momentum alone gives one equation for two unknowns. The second comes from how bouncy the impact is, described by the coefficient of restitution e:

v2′​−v1′​=−e(v2​−v1​).

e=1 is perfectly elastic (no energy lost), e=0 is perfectly plastic (the bodies stick together). Real values: steel balls about 0.9, a tennis ball 0.75, a car crash near 0.1. The kinetic energy lost is

ΔT=21​(1−e2)m1​+m2​m1​m2​​(v1​−v2​)2.

Worked exampleTwo lab carts

Cart 1, 0.5 kg at 2 m/s, hits cart 2, 1.0 kg at rest.

  1. e=1: v1′​=−0.667 m/s (bounces back), v2′​=1.333 m/s, no energy lost.
  2. e=0.6: v1′​=−0.133, v2′​=1.067 m/s; 0.427 J lost, matching 21​(1−0.36)⋅31​⋅4.
  3. e=0: both move off at 0.667 m/s; 0.667 J lost, two thirds of the original energy.
  4. Momentum before and after agrees to machine precision in 10,000 random collisions (worst relative error 5×10−16).
  5. A ball with e=0.8 dropped from 1 m bounces to 0.64, 0.41, 0.26 m: each height is e2 times the last.

Exercise 1A railway shunting impact

A 30 t wagon rolling at 1.5 m/s hits a stationary 20 t wagon and they couple (e=0). Find the common speed, the energy absorbed by the buffers and coupling, and the average force if the impact lasts 0.4 s.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Common speed: 30⋅1.5/(30+20)=0.9 m/s.
  2. Energy lost: 21​⋅5030⋅20​⋅103⋅1.52=13.5 kJ.
  3. Impulse on the second wagon: 20000⋅0.9=18,000 N s, so the average force is 18000/0.4=45 kN.

quiz.explain: Momentum.

quiz.q: Energy absorbed (kJ) in that coupling.
quiz.explain: 21​μv2 with e=0.

quiz.q: Rebound speed (m/s) of cart 1 (0.5 kg, 2 m/s) hitting 1.0 kg at rest with e=0.6, with sign. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Momentum plus restitution.

quiz.q: Airbags reduce injuries because they…
quiz.explain: Same impulse, longer time.
options: Increase the stopping time, lowering the force

quiz.q: In a collision with e=1 between equal masses, one at rest…
quiz.explain: Newton’s cradle.
options: The moving one bounces back at full speed

07.05.title: The rocket equation
07.05.html:
A rocket pushes itself forward by throwing mass backward. As it burns fuel it gets lighter, so the same thrust accelerates it harder. Newton’s law in its plain form assumes constant mass, so rockets need a careful derivation, and the result explains why rockets are mostly fuel and why they have stages.

Momentum over a short time

At time t the rocket has mass m and speed v. In dt it ejects mass dme​ backwards at speed ve​ relative to itself. With no outside forces, total momentum stays the same:

mv=(m−dme​)(v+dv)+dme​(v−ve​).

Expanding and dropping the tiny product dme​dv gives mdv=ve​dme​. The thrust is ve​m˙e​. Since dme​=−dm:

dv=−ve​mdm​⇒Δv=ve​lnm1​m0​​.

This is Tsiolkovsky’s rocket equation. The speed gained depends only on the exhaust speed and the mass ratio, not on how fast the fuel burns.

Gravity

Flying straight up with gravity, mv˙=m˙e​ve​−mg. Integrating over the burn time tb​ gives Δv=ve​ln(m0​/m1​)−gtb​. The gravity loss gtb​ is why rockets burn hard and fast at lift-off.

Why stages

The logarithm is cruel. Reaching low Earth orbit needs about 9.3 km/s including gravity and drag losses. With a good kerosene engine, ve​≈3 km/s, so m0​/m1​=e3.1≈22: 95 % of the rocket must be propellant. Dropping empty tanks and engines along the way (staging) means the later stages don’t have to accelerate dead weight.

Worked exampleA sounding rocket

Lift-off mass 1000 kg, 750 kg of propellant, ve​=2500 m/s, burning 15 kg/s for 50 s.

  1. Tsiolkovsky: Δv=2500ln(1000/250)=3465.736 m/s. RK4 on mv˙=m˙ve​ gives the same to 10−6 m/s.
  2. With gravity: burnout at 54.98 km and 2975.2 m/s. The difference is exactly gtb​=490.5 m/s.
  3. Thrust is 37.5 kN, a thrust-to-weight ratio of 3.82 at lift-off.
  4. Staging: drop a 60 kg tank after 500 kg of propellant and the same rocket reaches 3832 m/s instead of 3466 m/s.
  5. Coasting without drag would carry it to 506 km. Real sounding rockets of this size reach far less, because of air drag and the fact that real ones carry payloads.

Exercise 1How much propellant?

A spacecraft of 2000 kg (dry) needs a Δv of 1500 m/s for an orbit change. Its engine has ve​=3100 m/s. How much propellant must it carry?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. m0​/m1​=e1500/3100=e0.4839=1.6224.
  2. m0​=1.6224⋅2000=3245 kg, so it needs 1245 kg of propellant: 38 % of the fuelled mass.

quiz.explain: m1​(eΔv/ve​−1).

quiz.q: Gravity loss (m/s) for a 50 s vertical burn.
quiz.explain: gtb​.

quiz.q: Doubling the mass ratio of a rocket adds to its Δv…

A fixed ve​ln2
Four times the Δv

quiz.q: Rockets use stages mainly to…

options: Stop accelerating empty tanks and engines

07.06.title: Systems of particles
07.06.html:
A car is thousands of parts, a rocket sheds exhaust, a gymnast moves her arms in mid-air. Treating each as one particle seems too crude. Yet one result makes it legitimate for the overall motion: the centre of mass moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted on it.

The centre of mass theorem

For particles i with masses mi​ at positions ri​, define the total mass M and the centre of mass

rG​=M1​i∑​mi​ri​.

Write Newton’s law for each particle, splitting forces into external Fi​ and internal fij​ (from particle j on i):

mi​r¨i​=Fi​+j=i∑​fij​.

Add all of them. By Newton’s third law fij​=−fji​, so the internal forces cancel in pairs:

Mr¨G​=i∑​Fi​.

Consequences

  • With no external force, the centre of mass moves in a straight line at constant speed, and total momentum Mr˙G​ is conserved. That’s what made the collision problems of 07.04 solvable.
  • A diver can’t change the path of her centre of mass in the air: it follows a parabola whatever she does with her body.
  • An exploding firework’s fragments scatter, but their centre of mass continues along the original parabola (until fragments hit the ground).

N-body simulation

A good test of any simulation of interacting particles: the internal forces must sum to zero at every step, and momentum must stay constant to rounding error. The velocity Verlet method, used for molecular dynamics and planetary motion, keeps this property exactly.

Worked exampleFive bodies

Five masses between 0.5 and 2.0 (total 5.200) with random positions and velocities, attracting each other.

  1. Initial momentum (0.302751, 0.538379), so the centre of mass moves at (0.0582, 0.1035).
  2. After 5000 velocity-Verlet steps the momentum is unchanged to 6 decimals and beyond, and the centre of mass is within 3×10−14 of the straight line.
  3. The sum of mi​ai​ at the start is (−2×10−15,−1×10−15): zero up to rounding.
  4. With a uniform external gravity of 1 downward, the centre of mass lands at (−0.059615,−11.959423) after 5 time units, exactly the single-particle prediction r0​+vG​t+21​gt2.

Exercise 1A boat and a walker

A 70 kg person walks 4 m from the stern to the bow of a 210 kg boat floating at rest. Ignoring water resistance, how far does the boat move?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. No horizontal external force, and everything starts at rest: the centre of mass stays put.
  2. If the boat moves x backwards, the person moves 4−x forwards relative to the water: 70(4−x)=210x.
  3. x=280/280=1.0 m. The person moves 3.0 m relative to the water.

quiz.q: Distance (m) the 210 kg boat moves when a 70 kg person walks 4 m along it.
quiz.explain: The centre of mass stays put.

quiz.q: Centre of mass position (m) of 2 kg at x=0 and 3 kg at x=5.
quiz.explain: ∑mi​xi​/M.

quiz.q: A 4 kg firework at 30 m/s explodes into 1 kg and 3 kg pieces. The 1 kg piece moves at 60 m/s in the original direction. Speed (m/s) of the 3 kg piece.
quiz.explain: Momentum is conserved.

quiz.q: Why do internal forces drop out of the centre of mass equation?

options: They cancel in pairs by Newton’s third law

quiz.q: A diver tucks during a dive. Her centre of mass…
quiz.explain: Only gravity acts externally.

07.07.title: Angular momentum of particles
07.07.html:
A figure skater pulls in her arms and spins faster. A satellite moves fastest when closest to Earth. A ball on a string wound around a pole speeds up as the string shortens. All three follow from one law: the rate of change of angular momentum equals the applied moment, and if the moment is zero, angular momentum is conserved.

Angular momentum

For a particle of mass m at position r (from a fixed point O) with velocity v:

LO​=r×mv.

In the plane, with polar coordinates, L=mr2θ˙: only the transverse velocity rθ˙ counts.

The law

Differentiate: L˙O​=r˙×mv+r×mv˙. The first term is zero (a vector crossed with itself), and mv˙=F, so

L˙O​=r×F=MO​.

A central force, always pointing towards or away from O (string tension, gravity from a planet), has no moment about O. Then mr2θ˙ is constant.

The shrinking string

A mass whirls on a string pulled in through a hole. The string pulls radially, so L is conserved and

ω=ω0​(rr0​​)2.

Halve the radius and the spin rate quadruples. Kinetic energy is not conserved: it grows as 1/r2, and the extra energy comes from the work done pulling the string against the growing tension mrω2.

Worked examplePulling in the string

m=0.2 kg, r0​=0.8 m, ω0​=2π rad/s. The string is pulled in at 0.15 m/s for 4 s, to 0.2 m.

  1. RK4 on the transverse polar equation rθ¨+2r˙θ˙=0: ω rises to 100.531 rad/s (16 rev/s), as predicted by ω0​(r0​/r)2=16ω0​.
  2. L=0.804248 kg m²/s before and after, a relative change of 2×10−12.
  3. Kinetic energy rises from 2.527 J to 40.426 J. The difference, 37.899 J, equals ∫mrω2dr, the work done on the string.
  4. The tension climbs from 6.32 N to 404 N. Pulling in a fast-spinning mass gets very hard.

Exercise 1A satellite’s speed

A satellite in an elliptical orbit is 7000 km from Earth’s centre at perigee, moving at 8.0 km/s perpendicular to the radius. At apogee it is 10,500 km away. How fast is it moving there?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Gravity is central, so L=mrv⊥​ is conserved. At perigee and apogee the velocity is perpendicular to the radius.
  2. va​=vp​rp​/ra​=8.0⋅7000/10500=5.33 km/s.

quiz.q: Spin rate (rad/s) when the string is pulled from 0.8 m to 0.4 m, starting at 2π rad/s. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: ω0​(r0​/r)2.

quiz.explain: rp​vp​=ra​va​.

quiz.explain: mr2ω.

quiz.explain: Central force, zero moment.

07.08.title: Rigid body kinematics in 2D
07.08.html:
Windscreen wipers, bicycle suspensions, excavator arms, sewing machines and the pedals of a cross-trainer are linkages: rigid links joined by pins. Designing them means knowing where every point goes and how fast, for every input angle. One equation, applied link by link, does it.

Velocity of two points on one body

A rigid body moving in the plane has one angular velocity ω (the same for every line drawn on it). For two points A and B on it:

vB​=vA​+ω×rAB​.

The relative velocity ω×rAB​ is perpendicular to AB with size ω∣AB∣. Differentiating again:

aB​=aA​+α×rAB​−ω2rAB​.

The last term is the centripetal part, pointing from B back towards A.

The four-bar linkage

Four links in a loop: ground d, crank a, coupler b, rocker c. Given the crank angle:

  1. Position: joint A is on the crank circle; joint B is where the circle of radius b about A meets the circle of radius c about the rocker pivot.
  2. Velocity: write vB​ twice, once through the coupler (vA​+ω3​×rAB​) and once through the rocker (ω4​×rO4​B​). Equating them gives two equations for ω3​ and ω4​.

Grashof’s rule

Will the crank turn all the way round, or jam? Sort the link lengths: shortest s, longest l, the others p, q. If

s+l≤p+q,

the linkage is Grashof and at least one link can turn fully relative to the others. With the shortest link as the crank, the crank turns fully and the rocker swings back and forth: a crank-rocker. If s+l>p+q, no link can make a full turn.

Worked exampleA wiper-style linkage

a=20, b=70, c=45, d=70 mm. Sorted: 20 + 70 = 90 ≤ 45 + 70 = 115: Grashof, with the crank shortest.

  1. At 60° and 1 rev/s: A = (10, 17.321), B = (74.387, 44.786).
  2. Solving the velocity equations: ω3​=−0.8456, ω4​=1.9114 rad/s; ∣vA​∣=125.66 mm/s, ∣vB​∣=86.01 mm/s.
  3. Differentiating the rocker angle numerically gives the same ω4​ to 10−5.
  4. Over one crank turn the rocker swings 55.4°, between 79.3° and 134.6°.
  5. In 400 random linkages with the shortest link as the crank, Grashof’s rule predicted full rotation correctly every time.

Exercise 1Which linkage turns?

For each set (crank listed first, then coupler, rocker, ground, in mm), say whether the crank can turn fully: (a) 30, 80, 60, 70; (b) 40, 50, 60, 90; (c) 50, 30, 60, 70.

Show step-by-step solution

07.09.title: Planar rigid body dynamics
07.09.html:
Roll a solid disc and a hoop of the same mass and radius down a ramp, and the disc wins every time. Mass and radius don’t matter at all. What matters is how the mass is spread around the axis. Explaining this needs Newton’s law for rotation as well as translation.

Equations of motion in the plane

A rigid body in plane motion has three degrees of freedom: two for the centre of mass G and one for rotation. Three equations:

∑Fx​=maGx​,∑Fy​=maGy​,∑MG​=IG​α.

IG​ is the moment of inertia about G (next lesson). Moments must be taken about G, or about a fixed point, or else extra terms appear.

Rolling without slipping

A wheel of radius r rolling without slipping has its contact point momentarily at rest, so vG​=ωr and aG​=αr. That is the rolling constraint. Friction at the contact supplies the moment that spins the wheel up, and does no work, since the contact point doesn’t move.

Down a ramp

Write IG​=kmr2. Along the ramp: ma=mgsinθ−F. About G: Fr=IG​α=kmr2⋅a/r. Eliminate F:

a=1+kgsinθ​,F=1+kk​mgsinθ.

Solid sphere (k=2/5): a=75​gsinθ. Solid disc (k=1/2): 32​gsinθ. Thin ring (k=1): 21​gsinθ. The bigger k, the more of the energy goes into spinning rather than moving.

To roll without slipping, the friction needed must be available: F≤μN=μmgcosθ, which gives μ≥1+kk​tanθ.

Worked exampleThe race at 10°

A 2 m ramp at 10°, gsinθ=1.7035 m/s².

  1. Sliding block (no friction): 1.7035 m/s², 1.532 s.
  2. Solving the two equations for each shape: sphere 1.2168 m/s² (1.813 s), disc 1.1357 m/s² (1.877 s), ring 0.8517 m/s² (2.167 s). The disc’s acceleration is exactly 32​gsinθ, the ring’s 21​gsinθ.
  3. Energy check for the disc: mgh=21​mv2+21​Iω2=43​mv2 gives v=4gh/3​=2.1313 m/s, the same as the simulation.
  4. Friction needed per kg: disc 0.568 N, ring 0.852 N. The disc rolls without slipping if μ≥tan10°/3=0.0588.

A yo-yo is a solid disc of mass m and radius R with its string wound round an axle of radius r=R/4. Released from rest with the string held fixed, what is its downward acceleration and the string tension?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Down: ma=mg−T. About G: Tr=21​mR2α, with the constraint a=αr.
  2. So T=21​mR2a/r2=8ma (using R/r=4).
  3. ma=mg−8ma gives a=g/9=1.09 m/s², and T=98​mg.

07.10.title: Moment of inertia
07.10.html:
Mass tells you how hard it is to push something into motion; the moment of inertia tells you how hard it is to spin it. A flywheel stores energy by having a large one, a racing wheel accelerates quickly by having a small one, and a figure skater changes hers by moving her arms. It depends on where the mass sits, not only how much there is.

Definition

For a body rotating about an axis, each bit of mass dm at distance r from the axis contributes r2dm:

I=∫r2dm.

The radius of gyration k is defined by I=mk2: the radius at which all the mass could sit to give the same I.

Standard results

Body (axis) I
Thin ring, radius R mR2
Solid disc or cylinder 21​mR2
Thick ring, radii R1​, R2​ 21​m(R12​+R22​)
Solid sphere 52​mR2
Slender rod, about its centre 121​mL2

The parallel-axis theorem

If IG​ is about an axis through the centre of mass, then about a parallel axis a distance d away:

I=IG​+md2.

A small mass far from the axis matters far more than its own spin.

From a drawing

For a wheel symmetric about its axis with thickness t(r), a thin ring at radius r has dm=ρt(r)2πrdr, so I=∫ρt(r)2πr3dr. That one integral handles any profile. It’s what CAD mass-properties tools compute, and a check against simple shapes proves the code.

Worked exampleChecking shapes, then an engine flywheel

Steel, ρ=7850 kg/m³.

  1. Solid disc 400 × 30 mm: m=29.594 kg, I=0.591876 kg m², equal to 21​mR2.
  2. Ring from 300 to 400 mm diameter, 30 mm thick: m=12.947 kg, I=0.404603 kg m², equal to 21​m(R12​+R22​).
  3. A flywheel for a stationary engine: hub 60 mm wide from a 30 mm bore to 60 mm diameter, a 20 mm web out to 320 mm diameter, then a 60 mm rim to 400 mm. m=34.49 kg, I=0.86087 kg m², radius of gyration 158 mm.
  4. The rim is 62 % of the mass but 81 % of the inertia.
  5. A 0.5 kg balance mass bolted on at 150 mm adds 0.5⋅0.152=0.01125 kg m² by the parallel-axis term; its spin about its own axis adds only 2.5×10−5.
  6. At 3000 rpm the flywheel stores 21​Iω2=42.48 kJ.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Rim and tyre: 0.45⋅0.332=0.0490 kg m².
  2. Spokes: a rod from 0.03 to 0.33 m has I=3m​⋅r2​−r1​r23​−r13​​=30.006​⋅0.30.035937−0.000027​=2.394×10−4 kg m² each; 32 of them: 0.00766 kg m².
  3. Hub, as a solid cylinder: 21​⋅0.3⋅0.032=0.000135 kg m².
  4. Total about 0.0568 kg m². The rim dominates, which is why light rims matter so much to climbers.

07.11.title: Rotating machinery and balancing
07.11.html:
A washing machine walking across the floor, a car steering wheel shaking at 110 km/h, a fan humming loudly: all are unbalanced rotors. A few grams off-centre on something spinning at thousands of rpm produce forces of tens or hundreds of newtons, shaking bearings to pieces. Balancing is how every wheel, fan, turbine and crankshaft is made smooth.

The force from a small unbalance

A mass m at radius r on a shaft spinning at ω needs a centripetal force mrω2, supplied by the bearings. The force rotates with the shaft, so the bearings feel it as a vibration at the running speed. The quantity that matters is mr, the unbalance, usually in g mm or g m.

For several masses, add the vectors: U=∑mi​ri​ei​. The rotor is statically balanced if U=0: it then stays put at any angle when resting on knife edges.

Dynamic unbalance

Static balance is not enough for a long rotor. Two equal masses on opposite sides at different positions along the shaft cancel each other’s force, but they make a rotating couple ∑mi​ri​zi​ei​ that rocks the rotor in its bearings. A rotor is dynamically balanced only if both the force and the moment vanish:

∑mi​ri​ei​=0,∑mi​ri​zi​ei​=0.

Two-plane balancing

Any unbalance can be cancelled with one correction mass in each of two chosen planes, zL​ and zR​. With unknown correction vectors uL​, uR​:

uL​+uR​=−U,zL​uL​+zR​uR​=−M.

Two vector equations, two vector unknowns. Balancing machines measure the bearing forces and solve exactly this. Car tyre fitters do it with clip-on weights on the inner and outer rim edges.

Worked exampleBalancing a fan rotor

Three unbalances: 20 g at 100 mm, 30°, z=0.1 m; 15 g at 120 mm, 160°, z=0.3 m; 10 g at 80 mm, 270°, z=0.5 m.

  1. Resultant unbalance 0.817 g m, which at 3000 rpm makes the bearings carry 80.6 N.
  2. A single correction mass in the middle plane cancels the force (residual 5×10−20) but leaves a couple of 0.500 g m².
  3. Two-plane correction at radius 0.1 m: 11.72 g at −120.7° in the plane z=0, and 5.89 g at 19.0° in the plane z=0.6 m.
  4. Afterwards force and moment are both below 10−18, zero to rounding.

Exercise 1A car wheel

A car wheel spins at 110 km/h with a 0.31 m rolling radius. A 25 g balance weight has fallen off the rim at radius 0.20 m. What rotating force does the missing weight cause?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ω=v/r=30.56/0.31=98.6 rad/s.
  2. F=mrω2=0.025⋅0.20⋅98.62=48.6 N, rotating at 15.7 Hz.
  3. That is enough to shake the steering wheel noticeably: this is the classic “wobble at motorway speed”.

07.12.title: Relative motion and rotating frames
07.12.html:
Roll a ball across a turning playground roundabout and, from the roundabout, it curves away as if pushed. Seen from the ground, it went straight. Engineers meet this whenever they measure from something that moves: sensors on a spinning rotor, a robot arm on a turntable, weather on the rotating Earth. The fix is to add the right extra terms to the acceleration.

Velocity in a rotating frame

Let a frame rotate at angular velocity Ω about its origin. A point at r, moving with velocity vrel​ as seen in that frame, has inertial velocity

v=vrel​+Ω×r.

Acceleration

Differentiating again, with the same rule applied to vrel​:

a=arel​+2Ω×vrel​+Ω×(Ω×r)+Ω˙×r.
  • 2Ω×vrel​: the Coriolis term, only for things that move within the frame.
  • Ω×(Ω×r): the centripetal term, pointing to the axis, size Ω2r.
  • Ω˙×r: the term from a changing spin rate.

Fictitious forces

Writing F=ma in the rotating frame gives

marel​=F−2mΩ×vrel​−mΩ×(Ω×r).

The extra terms behave like forces: the Coriolis force and the centrifugal force. With Ω anticlockwise (seen from above), the Coriolis force pushes moving things to the right. The northern hemisphere rotates anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole, so winds and long-range shells deflect right there, and left in the southern hemisphere.

Worked exampleThe carousel ball

Ω=2π/6=1.047 rad/s anticlockwise. The ball is rolled from the centre at 2 m/s along the carousel’s x axis (no friction, no rolling resistance).

  1. In the inertial frame there is no horizontal force, so the ball goes straight at 2 m/s.
  2. The code integrates the rotating-frame equation with only the Coriolis and centrifugal terms. It matches the straight inertial line, transformed into the rotating frame, to 6×10−15 m.
  3. After 1.2 s the ball is at (0.742, −2.283) m on the carousel: deflected to the right. With the carousel turning clockwise it ends at (0.742, +2.283), deflected to the left.
  4. Early on, the sideways drift is Ωvt2: 0.02094 m at 0.1 s against 0.02091 m simulated.
  5. On Earth at 47° N, Ωsinφ=5.33×10−5 rad/s: a shell at 1000 m/s for 20 s drifts about 21 m.

Exercise 1A slider on a rotating arm

A robot arm turns at a constant 2 rad/s. A gripper slides outward along it at 0.5 m/s. At the instant it is 0.6 m from the axis, find its acceleration (assume the slide speed is constant).

Show step-by-step solution
  1. arel​=0 (constant slide speed along the arm), Ω˙=0.
  2. Centripetal: Ω2r=4⋅0.6=2.4 m/s² towards the axis.
  3. Coriolis: 2Ωvrel​=2⋅2⋅0.5=2.0 m/s², perpendicular to the arm in the direction of rotation.
  4. Total: 2.42+2.02​=3.12 m/s². The arm must push sideways on the gripper with m⋅2.0 m/s².

07.13.title: 3D rigid-body kinematics
07.13.html:
Drones, satellites, phones and VR headsets all need to know which way they point. Their gyroscopes measure angular velocity in body axes, many times a second, and software integrates that into an orientation. How orientation is stored matters: the obvious choice, three angles, fails at certain attitudes. Quaternions don’t.

Rotation matrices

An orientation can be stored as a 3 × 3 rotation matrix R that turns body-frame vectors into world-frame ones. It is orthogonal (RTR=I) with determinant +1. Nine numbers for three degrees of freedom: integrating it lets rounding errors break orthogonality.

Euler angles

Three successive rotations, for example yaw ψ, pitch θ and roll ϕ. Intuitive, and used on every aircraft display. But the angle rates relate to body rates (p,q,r) through

ϕ˙​=p+(qsinϕ+rcosϕ)tanθ,ψ˙​=cosθqsinϕ+rcosϕ​.

At θ=90°, cosθ=0: the rates become infinite. Two of the gimbal axes line up and one degree of freedom is lost. That is gimbal lock, which nearly caught Apollo 13’s guidance platform.

Quaternions

A unit quaternion q=(cos2α​, sin2α​n) represents a rotation by α about the unit axis n. Four numbers, one constraint (∣q∣=1), no singularities. With body angular velocity ω:

q˙​=21​q⊗(0,ω).

This is linear in q and smooth everywhere. Integrate with RK4 and renormalise q after each step to keep ∣q∣=1. Convert to a rotation matrix or Euler angles only for display.

Worked exampleIntegrating orientation

  1. Constant spin of 1.5 rad/s about the axis (1, 2, 2)/3 for 4 s: the integrated quaternion matches the exact axis-angle rotation to 1×10−14.
  2. A tumbling body (ω varying with time) for 200 s with a coarse 0.05 s step: with renormalisation the norm error stays at 2×10−16; without it, it drifts to 1.9×10−7. Small, but it grows without bound in long flights.
  3. The rotation matrix built from the final quaternion is orthogonal to 3×10−16, determinant 1.
  4. Euler-angle rates for a 1 rad/s body yaw (roll 0.3 rad): 0.96 rad/s of yaw rate at level pitch, 10.96 at 85°, 54.7 at 89°, 547 at 89.9°.

  2. q⊗(0,1,0,0)=(0,0.7071,0.7071,0).
  3. Multiply by q∗=(0.7071,0,0,−0.7071): (0,0,1,0). So v′=(0,1,0), the x axis turned 90° onto the y axis, as expected.

07.14.title: Inertia tensor
07.14.html:
In plane motion one number, I, describes how a body resists spinning. In 3D the body can spin about any axis, and a single number can’t capture that. A tilted block, a crankshaft or a satellite with solar panels all need the inertia tensor: a 3 × 3 matrix whose eigenvectors are the body’s natural spin axes.

Angular momentum in 3D

For a rigid body spinning at ω, summing r×m(ω×r) over all its mass gives

HG​=Iω,I=∫(∣r∣21−rrT)dm.

Written out:

I=​Ixx​−Ixy​−Ixz​​−Ixy​Iyy​−Iyz​​−Ixz​−Iyz​Izz​​​,Ixx​=∫(y2+z2)dm,Ixy​=∫xydm.

The off-diagonal products of inertia mean H is generally not parallel to ω. Spin a lopsided wheel and its angular momentum points off-axis. Keeping it turning then needs a rotating moment from the bearings: the dynamic unbalance of 07.11.

Principal axes

I is symmetric, so it has three real eigenvalues and three perpendicular eigenvectors. Along those principal axes the products of inertia vanish and H is parallel to ω. The eigenvalues are the principal moments I1​≤I2​≤I3​. Turning the body changes every entry of I in a fixed frame, but not the eigenvalues. Axes of symmetry are always principal axes.

Worked exampleA block and a bracket

  1. A solid block 0.4 × 0.2 × 0.1 m of 8 kg as a cloud of 200,000 random points: diagonal of I = (0.03336, 0.11358, 0.13361) kg m², against the exact 12m​(b2+c2) etc. = (0.03333, 0.11333, 0.13333). The cloud is within 0.25 %.
  2. Turn the block by 30° about z: Ixx​=0.05346, Iyy​=0.09348 and an off-diagonal entry of −0.03476 kg m² appear.
  3. The eigenvalues are unchanged, (0.03336, 0.11358, 0.13361), and the axis of least inertia points at 30.04° (the block’s long edge, within sampling noise).
  4. Three point masses (1, 2, 1.5 kg) forming an L-shaped bracket: centre of mass (0.1333, 0.0667, 0.0333) m, principal moments (0.02377, 0.12623, 0.15000) kg m².

  2. In the x-y block, (0.18−0.18​−0.180.18​) has eigenvalues 0 and 0.36.
  3. The eigenvalue 0 belongs to (1,1,0)/2​, the dumbbell’s own axis (point masses on it have no inertia about it). The others are 0.36 about (1,−1,0)/2​ and 0.36 about z.

07.15.title: Euler's equations
07.15.html:
Toss a phone or a tennis racket in the air spinning about each of its three axes in turn. About the long axis and the flat axis it spins cleanly. About the third, the intermediate axis, it flips over every time, however carefully you throw it. In 1985 a Soviet cosmonaut saw a wing nut do the same in orbit. Euler’s equations explain why.

The equations

In body-fixed principal axes, H=(I1​ω1​,I2​ω2​,I3​ω3​). The axes rotate with the body, so differentiating H needs the rotating-frame rule of 07.12: H˙=H˙rel​+ω×H=M. In components:

I1​ω˙1​−(I2​−I3​)ω2​ω3​I2​ω˙2​−(I3​−I1​)ω3​ω1​I3​ω˙3​−(I1​−I2​)ω1​ω2​​=M1​=M2​=M3​​

They are nonlinear: the spin about one axis feeds the others. Even with no moment at all, ω can change in body axes.

Stability of steady spin

Take M=0, spin Ω about axis 2 and small wobbles ω1​, ω3​. Linearising:

ω¨1​=I1​I3​(I2​−I1​)(I3​−I2​)​Ω2ω1​.

With I1​<I2​<I3​ the coefficient is positive: the wobble grows exponentially at rate λ=Ω(I2​−I1​)(I3​−I2​)/(I1​I3​)​. Spin is unstable about the intermediate axis. About axis 1 or axis 3 the coefficient is negative and the wobble just oscillates: stable. This is the tennis racket theorem.

Kinetic energy 21​∑Ii​ωi2​ and the size of H are both conserved, a good check on any simulation.

Worked exampleA tumbling phone

I=(1.0,2.5,3.3)×10−4 kg m², spin 10 rad/s, initial wobble 10−3 rad/s on the other two axes, 10 s of RK4 with a 1 ms step.

  1. About the smallest axis: the wobble grows only 1.7 times (it oscillates). About the largest: 1.5 times.
  2. About the intermediate axis: the wobble grows 9325 times and the main spin reverses 3 times in 10 s. The body flips.
  3. Linear theory: λ=101.5⋅0.8/(1.0⋅3.3)​=6.03 s⁻¹, so the wobble doubles every 0.115 s.
  4. Energy and ∣H∣ stay constant to better than 10−12 in all three runs.

Exercise 1A spinning satellite

A satellite has principal moments 800, 1000 and 1200 kg m². It spins at 0.5 rad/s about the 1000 kg m² axis. How fast does a small wobble grow? What would you change?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Intermediate axis: λ=0.5(1000−800)(1200−1000)/(800⋅1200)​=0.540000/960000​=0.102 s⁻¹.
  2. A wobble doubles every ln2/0.102=6.8 s: in a few minutes the satellite tumbles.
  3. Spin it about the 1200 kg m² axis (the largest) instead. With some energy dissipation (flexing antennas, fuel slosh), only the largest axis is stable in the long run, as Explorer 1 showed in 1958.

07.16.title: Gyroscopes and precession
07.16.html:
Hold a spinning bicycle wheel by one end of its axle and let go of the other. Instead of falling, it swings slowly round in a horizontal circle. That is precession, and it’s what stabilises spinning tops, points ship gyrocompasses north, steers satellites with control moment gyros, and partly explains why a moving bike is easy to balance.

The fast-top approximation

A rotor spins fast at ω about its axis, with moment of inertia I3​, so it carries angular momentum H=I3​ω along the axis. Its centre of mass is a distance l from a pivot, with the axis horizontal. Gravity makes a torque M=mgl, horizontal and perpendicular to the axis.

By H˙=M, the torque changes H sideways, not downwards. The tip of H moves in a horizontal circle at rate Ω, with ∣H˙∣=ΩH:

Ω=I3​ωmgl​.

Faster spin means slower precession. Double the torque and it precesses twice as fast.

Nutation

The formula assumes all the angular momentum comes from the spin. Released from rest, the gyroscope first dips slightly, then bobs up and down while it precesses. This wobble, nutation, has an amplitude roughly proportional to 1/ω2. It fades quickly for a fast rotor and the steady precession takes over. Simulating the full equations of the heavy top (from its Lagrangian, as in 07.18) shows both effects.

Gyroscopic moments in machines

When a spinning part is forced to turn its axis at rate Ω, the bearings must supply a moment I3​ωΩ. Turbine rotors in turning ships, propellers on manoeuvring aircraft and car wheels during steering all feel it.

Worked exampleA toy gyroscope

m=0.15 kg, l=0.04 m, I3​=6×10−5 kg m², I1​=4×10−5 kg m² about the pivot, released horizontally from rest.

  1. Formula at 1000 rad/s: Ω=0.15⋅9.81⋅0.04/(6×10−5⋅1000)=0.981 rad/s.
  2. Simulated average precession over 2 s: 9.702 rad/s at 100 rad/s spin (ratio 0.989), 0.98092 at 1000 rad/s (0.9999), 0.49055 at 2000 rad/s (1.0001).
  3. Nutation amplitude: 7.39° at 100 rad/s, 0.30° at 500, 0.019° at 2000. Four times the spin gives about one sixteenth of the wobble.
  4. At 2000 rad/s (19,100 rpm) it precesses once every 12.8 s.

Exercise 1A ship’s turbine

A ship’s turbine rotor has I=900 kg m² and spins at 3600 rpm with its axis fore and aft. The ship turns at 2° per second. What gyroscopic moment do the bearings carry?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ω=3600⋅2π/60=377 rad/s, so H=900⋅377=3.39×105 kg m²/s.
  2. Ω=2° per s=0.0349 rad/s.
  3. M=HΩ=3.39×105⋅0.0349=11.8 kN m, acting in the vertical plane through the axis (it tries to pitch the rotor).

07.17.title: Flywheel energy storage
07.17.html:
A flywheel stores energy as rotation. Spin it up with spare power, draw the power back when needed. Modern ones smooth the grid, recover braking energy in buses and racing cars, and keep data centres running for the seconds before a generator starts. How much they can store is limited by one thing: how fast the rim can go before it flies apart.

Energy

E=21​Iω2.

For a thin rim of mass m at radius R, I=mR2 and E=21​mv2 with rim speed v=ωR. Energy grows with the square of speed, so flywheels spin fast: 20,000 to 50,000 rpm.

Rim stress

Cut a thin spinning rim in half. Each half needs a centripetal force, supplied by tension in the two cut faces, just like the pressure vessel of 06.21. A rim element of mass ρARdθ needs ρARdθ⋅Rω2 inward. Summing the components across the cut gives 2ρAR2ω2=2σA, so

σ=ρR2ω2=ρv2.

The hoop stress depends only on the rim speed and the density. Setting σ to the material strength gives a burst speed vmax​=σ/ρ​, the same for a small or a large wheel.

Specific energy

At the limit, the energy per kilogram of rim is

e=2vmax2​​=2ρσ​.

Size doesn’t matter; only the material’s strength-to-density ratio does. That’s why high-performance flywheels use carbon fibre rather than steel. And since stress grows with speed squared, a 10 % overspeed means 21 % more stress. Flywheels sit in strong containment housings.

Worked exampleSteel against carbon fibre

  1. High-strength steel, ρ=7850 kg/m³, usable stress 800 MPa: vmax​=319.2 m/s. At R=0.2, 0.5 and 1.0 m that is 15,242, 6097 and 3048 rpm. Cutting the rim in half and integrating the centrifugal load numerically gives exactly 800.00 MPa each time.
  2. Specific energy at the limit: steel 51.0 kJ/kg (14.2 Wh/kg); carbon fibre at 1.5 GPa and 1600 kg/m³: 468.8 kJ/kg (130.2 Wh/kg).
  3. A 60 kg carbon rim at 0.25 m radius, with a safety factor of 1.5 on stress: top speed 30,198 rpm (rim speed 791 m/s), storing 5.21 kWh. Running between 50 % and 100 % speed releases three quarters of that: 3.91 kWh.
  4. These are ideal thin-rim figures. Hubs, bearings and the containment cut the real system’s energy density several times.

Exercise 1A cast-iron flywheel

An old engine has a cast-iron flywheel (ρ=7200 kg/m³, safe hoop stress 20 MPa) with a rim of mean radius 0.9 m. What is the safe maximum speed in rpm? If the rim has mass 400 kg, how much energy does it hold at that speed?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. vmax​=20×106/7200​=52.7 m/s.
  2. ω=52.7/0.9=58.6 rad/s, which is 559 rpm.
  3. E=21​⋅400⋅52.72=556 kJ, about 0.15 kWh. Cast iron is weak in tension, so these flywheels ran slowly.

07.18.title: Lagrangian mechanics
07.18.html:
Newton’s method needs every force, including the constraint forces at pins and guides that you don’t care about. For a double pendulum, a robot arm or a crank mechanism this gets messy fast. Lagrange’s method works with energies in a set of coordinates that already respect the constraints, and the constraint forces never appear.

Generalised coordinates

Pick the minimum number of coordinates q1​,…,qn​ that fix the configuration. A double pendulum needs two angles, θ1​ and θ2​, not four Cartesian positions linked by two rod-length constraints. The number n is the number of degrees of freedom.

The Lagrangian

Write the kinetic energy T and potential energy V in terms of the qi​ and their rates q˙​i​, and form

L=T−V.

Then for each coordinate

dtd​(∂q˙​i​∂L​)−∂qi​∂L​=Qi​,

where Qi​ is the generalised force from anything not in V (applied torques, damping). For a conservative system Qi​=0. This gives n equations of motion with no reaction forces.

A check on one pendulum

For a single pendulum, T=21​ml2θ˙2 and V=−mglcosθ. Then ∂L/∂θ˙=ml2θ˙, its time derivative is ml2θ¨, and ∂L/∂θ=−mglsinθ. The equation is ml2θ¨+mglsinθ=0, the familiar result, with no rod tension needed.

The double pendulum

With two equal masses on equal rods the differentiation is tedious by hand but trivial for a computer algebra system. The code below lets SymPy derive both equations, then integrates them. For small swings the system has two normal modes, at ω=(2∓2​)g/l​. For large swings it’s chaotic: tiny differences in the start grow exponentially, though energy is still conserved.

Worked exampleDeriving and testing the double pendulum

m1​=m2​=1 kg, l1​=l2​=1 m, g=9.81 m/s².

  1. SymPy forms L, applies Lagrange’s equation to each angle and solves for θ¨1​,θ¨2​.
  2. Small swing in the in-phase mode shape (θ2​=2​θ1​): simulated period 2.6211 s, theory 2π/(2−2​)9.81​=2.6211 s.
  3. Large swing from 2.0 and 2.5 rad, 20 s with RK4: relative energy drift 4.2×10−4 at Δt=0.01 s, 9.4×10−9 at 0.001 s. The equations are right; the step size controls the error.
  4. Two starts differing by 10−9 rad differ by more than 0.1 rad in θ2​ after 9.73 s. Long-term prediction is impossible in principle.

Exercise 1A bead on a spinning hoop

A bead of mass m slides without friction on a hoop of radius R spinning about its vertical diameter at a constant Ω. Using the angle θ from the bottom, T=21​mR2(θ˙2+Ω2sin2θ) and V=−mgRcosθ. Find the equation of motion, and the angle where the bead can sit still when Ω=5 rad/s and R=0.2 m.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ∂L/∂θ˙=mR2θ˙; ∂L/∂θ=mR2Ω2sinθcosθ−mgRsinθ.
  2. Equation: Rθ¨=RΩ2sinθcosθ−gsinθ.
  3. Equilibrium off the bottom: cosθ=g/(RΩ2)=9.81/(0.2⋅25)=1.962. That’s more than 1, so at 5 rad/s the bead can only sit at the bottom.
  4. The off-centre equilibrium appears only above Ω=g/R​=7.0 rad/s. At 10 rad/s, cosθ=0.4905, so θ=60.6°.

07.19.title: Rail vehicles in curves
07.19.html:
A train can’t lean into a curve the way a cyclist does, and its wheels are held on by flanges only a few centimetres high. So the track does the leaning. The outer rail is raised (the cant, or superelevation) so that gravity supplies part of the centripetal force. Getting the cant right sets the comfortable speed, the wear on rails and wheels and the safety margin against overturning.

Balance speed

The track is tilted by angle ϕ, with sinϕ=h/S for cant h and rail-centre spacing S≈1.5 m on standard gauge. A vehicle at speed v on radius R needs centripetal acceleration v2/R toward the curve centre. Resolve along the tilted floor: the passengers feel a sideways acceleration

alat​=Rv2​cosϕ−gsinϕ.

It vanishes at the balance speed

vb​=gRtanϕ​.

At vb​ the resultant of gravity and centrifugal effect is square to the floor. Wheels, rails and passengers feel no sideways force.

Cant deficiency and excess

Mixed traffic can’t all run at one speed. A fast passenger train runs above vb​ and has cant deficiency: it would need more cant than is there, and its passengers feel pushed outward. A slow freight train runs below vb​ with cant excess, which loads the inner rail and wears it. Railways set limits, typically about 1.0 m/s² of uncompensated lateral acceleration for conventional trains (roughly 150 mm of deficiency) and up to 2 m/s² measured on the track for tilting trains, whose bodies lean further to keep passengers comfortable.

Overturning

At very high speed the resultant force moves past the outer rail, and the vehicle tips. The limit depends on the centre of mass height. It is far above the comfort limit, which is what actually sets the line speed.

Worked exampleA main-line curve

R=1200 m, cant 150 mm, S=1.5 m.

  1. Tilt ϕ=arcsin(0.150/1.5)=5.739°.
  2. Balance speed vb​=9.81⋅1200⋅tan5.739°​=34.40 m/s =123.8 km/h, where the in-floor acceleration is exactly zero.
  3. Lateral acceleration and cant deficiency (negative means excess): 80 km/h, −0.572 m/s² (−87 mm); 120 km/h, −0.060 (−8 mm); 160 km/h, +0.657 (+102 mm); 200 km/h, +1.578 (+243 mm).
  4. Speed limits: 176.0 km/h for a conventional train at 1.0 m/s², 215.9 km/h for a tilting train at 2.0 m/s².

Exercise 1Setting the cant

A new curve of radius 800 m will carry trains at 100 km/h. What cant gives balance at that speed? The maximum allowed cant is 160 mm. Is it within the limit?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. v=27.78 m/s, so tanϕ=v2/(gR)=771.6/7848=0.09832 and ϕ=5.615°.
  2. Cant h=Ssinϕ=1.5⋅0.09785=0.1468 m =147 mm.
  3. That is within 160 mm. In practice the cant is often set a little lower so slow trains don’t overload the inner rail.

07.20.title: Multibody simulation
07.20.html:
Car suspensions, robot arms, landing gear and engines are all collections of rigid bodies joined by pins, sliders and contacts. Multibody software (Adams, Simpack, the dynamics in many CAD packages) builds and solves their equations automatically. This lesson builds a small one for a slider-crank, the mechanism inside every piston engine and compressor.

Bodies and coordinates

Give each planar body three coordinates: the position of its centre of mass and its rotation, (xi​,yi​,θi​). A slider-crank has three moving bodies (crank, connecting rod, piston), so q has 9 entries. That is more than the one degree of freedom the mechanism really has. The extra coordinates are tied together by constraints.

Constraint equations

Each joint gives algebraic equations Φ(q)=0. A pin joint makes two points coincide (2 equations), a slider keeps a point on a line and stops rotation (2 equations), and pinning the crank to the ground takes 2 more. Here there are 8 equations for 9 coordinates, leaving 1 degree of freedom. Differentiating twice gives the acceleration-level constraint

Φq​q¨​=γ,γ=−(Φq​q˙​)q​q˙​,

where Φq​ is the Jacobian of the constraints.

Lagrange multipliers

The joints apply reaction forces ΦqT​λ, one multiplier per constraint equation. Newton’s laws for all bodies plus the constraints form one linear system:

[MΦq​​ΦqT​0​][q¨​λ​]=[Qγ​].

Solve it at every time step, then integrate q¨​. As a bonus, λ gives the bearing loads directly.

Drift and Baumgarte stabilisation

Integrating accelerations only enforces the constraints at acceleration level. Numerical error slowly lets the joints come apart. Baumgarte’s fix replaces γ by γ−2αΦ˙−β2Φ, which pulls any violation back toward zero like a stiff damped spring.

Worked exampleSimulating the slider-crank

r=0.05 m, l=0.15 m, masses 2, 1 and 0.5 kg, no gravity, no applied torque. Start at crank angle 0.3 rad and 600 rpm.

  1. Initial positions and velocities are solved to satisfy the constraints exactly: piston at x=197.037 mm, kinetic energy 8.2176 J. The analytic Jacobian agrees with finite differences to better than 10−9.
  2. 0.5 s with RK4 at Δt=0.5 ms: with no stabilisation the joints drift apart by up to 7.4×10−8 m; with Baumgarte (α=β=20) the worst is 2.1×10−9 m. Kinetic energy is conserved to 2.2×10−7.
  3. Even with no load, the crank speed is not constant. The effective inertia changes with angle, so at constant energy the speed must change: after 0.05 s the crank is at 3.0653 rad turning at 66.126 rad/s, up from 62.832. Engines carry flywheels partly to smooth this out.

Exercise 1Piston acceleration

Using x=rcosθ+l2−r2sin2θ​, the piston acceleration at top dead centre (θ=0) and constant crank speed ω is −rω2(1+r/l). For r=0.05 m, l=0.15 m and 6000 rpm, find it, and the inertia force on a 0.5 kg piston.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ω=6000⋅2π/60=628.3 rad/s.
  2. a=−0.05⋅628.32⋅(1+1/3)=−26,319 m/s², about 2700 g.
  3. F=0.5⋅26,319=13.2 kN. That load goes through the wrist pin and rod on every revolution, 100 times a second.
